01

Executive verdict

The strongest product idea is not “FPS in a browser.” It is a full competitive-FPS grammar made approachable by instant access and memorable by aggressively local comedy.

CORO SOLTO already behaves like a content-rich game, but it earns trust like a prototype: the solo combat loop is vivid and surprisingly complete, while rules, ranking integrity, multiplayer status, and UI consistency still contradict one another.

Why it works

The premise is immediately legible, the match setup is generous, kills feel emphatic, and every faction creates shareable character appeal without requiring install friction.

What blocks scale

Competitive products need authority. A how-to panel, match setup, scoreboard, ranking notice, and multiplayer browser currently communicate different levels of readiness.

Best next move

Turn the current solo sandbox into a trustworthy “practice season”: normalize rules, add difficulty and onboarding, label network capability honestly, then graduate to verified human matches.

02

Why this game

This is a useful teardown because its evidence is unusually rich: a complete playable session, a substantial public repository, and a creator post that states both ambition and missing pieces.

Selection rationale

  • Rare browser genre: a content-heavy 3D arena FPS, not a lightweight minigame.
  • Distinct positioning: Brazilian caricature factions and meme-radio flavor provide a recognizable cultural wrapper.
  • Reconstructable system: menu, settings, setup, selection, match HUD, death, scoring, victory and room discovery were all exposed.
  • Transparent production: the repository documents a multi-agent workflow, technical stack and content scale.

Evidence counterweight

It was selected for design and implementation legibility, not proven market momentum. Public play, retention and conversion metrics were unavailable. Repository volume—roughly 47.6K lines of game JavaScript in the indexed snapshot and 1,668 commits—is evidence of scope and iteration, not evidence of quality or demand.

Formula

Counter-Strike-like browser FPS × Brazilian satire × oversized AI-maintained content library. The differentiation comes from the multiplication, not any one factor.

04

Observed first session

The session completed the whole solo funnel and then inspected the network browser. It is therefore strong evidence for first-run UX and bot combat, but not for human multiplayer.

Orient

Settings, leaderboard, how-to, feedback, support and profile editing establish the shell before play.

Configure

Deathmatch is set to two per side, all weapons, Ferro Velho do Zé, with a custom nickname.

Express

The player chooses Clowns, previews characters and commits to Palhaço do Mal before selecting Team E as opponent.

Fight & close

Five rounds complete 5–0; the victory screen summarizes rounds, kills and deaths, then offers replay or menu return.

05

Core loop

The moment loop is conventional enough to be learned instantly; the content wrapper makes it proprietary.

Read radar & sightline→Move / peek→Choose weapon→Aim / fire→Damage / kill feedback→Reposition or respawn

Second-to-second

Scan minimap and lanes, manage range, swap between primary/pistol/knife, use scope where supported, reload, and collect dropped weapons through a contextual pickup.

Round

Accumulate team kills before the timer expires. Death triggers a short recap and rapid respawn, so the tempo stays continuous rather than elimination-based.

Match

Repeat on the same map, preserve cumulative kills/deaths, view team tables between rounds, then receive a faction-themed result and replay decision.

07

Mechanics & rules

Combat rules are readable in play; match rules need normalization. The observed match ran every configured round even after one side had an unbeatable lead.

Confirmed combat model

  • Health starts at 100 and damage is location/range/weapon dependent.
  • Headshots are presented as highly lethal.
  • Weapons expose magazine and reserve ammunition; reloads and pickups are supported.
  • Death shows killer, weapon, distance, damage and incoming direction before respawn.
  • Kill feed, damage numbers and streak banners layer immediate confirmation.
  • Team round score and personal cumulative kills/deaths persist across rounds.

Rule contradiction to resolve

The match setup labeled the configuration as five rounds; the help copy described a default first-to-three format; the observed game continued through all five rounds and finished 5–0. Reconstruction should represent these as two explicit settings: roundCount and winCondition = fixed | bestOf. Never infer one from the other.

Deathmatch

A round uses a visible countdown and a team kill target or higher score at expiry. Exact target calculation is not confirmed.

Capture

Public help describes no round clock: capture three flags or hold all, first to two rounds, with an overall match cap only surfaced late.

Spawn state

A freshly spawned bot appeared visually translucent during play, consistent with temporary protection. Duration and cancellation rules remain unknown.

Progression, economy & content

The observed product is breadth-led rather than economy-led. Variety is selected up front or found in the arena; no purchase loop was exposed.

Content architecture

Match setup filters the arsenal to All, Pistols, Knife or AWP, chooses team size from two to eight per side, cycles map, then splits faction and character selection into separate expressive steps. Each character carries rarity, prose, role and four rated attributes.

Persistence architecture

A local profile nickname feeds the kill feed and score table. Local statistics track matches, wins, K/D, arena time, kills, deaths, headshots and rounds. The global board is intentionally disabled until trustworthy. No currency, unlock cost, battle pass or inventory ownership was observed.

09

UX/UI reconstruction atlas

The interface combines an editorial, poster-like shell with a sparse competitive HUD. Rebuild them as related token families, not one universal component skin.

Viewport & responsive policy

Reference canvas: 1920×1080, 16:9. The game surface scales to cover while preserving a 16:9 safe area. At narrower ratios, maintain minimum 24px horizontal safe padding, collapse two-column lobby content, and keep combat corner clusters inside env(safe-area-inset-*). Under 960px width, present a desktop-controls requirement instead of compressing the FPS HUD into unusability.

Grid & density

Menu pages use a centered ~1180px content span, 32–48px section gaps and large negative space. Combat uses edge anchoring: 16–24px to minimap and health, 24–36px to score and weapon rail. Modal settings use a ~960×660 panel with a 20–24px interior rhythm.

Color tokens
VOID #070806
ACTION #C5EF26
INFO #44D5D7
STREAK #FF6948
DANGER #EF4F52
OPPONENT #AD79FF
Typography
Display: condensed uppercase, weight 800–900, 0.04–0.10em tracking. Telemetry: condensed mono/tech face, 600–900, 0.08–0.18em tracking. Body: neutral sans, 14–18px. Use numeric tabular figures for score, timer, ammo and tables.
Shape & motion
Mostly square black panels with hairline olive borders; primary buttons use a clipped lower-right corner. Hover: border and label brighten over 120ms. Page transition: 160–220ms fade/slide. Kill banners: 90ms scale-in, ~850ms hold, 180ms fade. Never animate critical score values with delay.

10

Feedback & presentation

The game is strongest when feedback is redundant: visual, spatial and tabular channels all confirm the same event.

Combat confirmation

Muzzle/weapon response, floating damage, kill feed, team score, personal kill count and streak banner make a kill difficult to miss. Blood pools remain as environmental history.

Navigation feedback

Lime highlights mark current weapon and primary actions; cyan marks informational/online elements; faction colors divide score tables. Selected states should always change shape or text as well as color.

Audio architecture

Master volume and meme voice lines are independently controlled. The actual mix, spatial attenuation, reload cadence and radio priority are unknown and must be tuned against gameplay, not inferred from screenshots.

11

Social, viral & return loops

The social shell is productively specific—regions, codes, named rooms and spectating—but the observed session does not validate a human match.

Visible social affordances

  • Nickname becomes public combat identity.
  • Invite-code input supports direct coordination.
  • Room cards expose matchup, mode, map, capacity, side join buttons and spectating.
  • Room creation chooses name, map rotation, two factions, mode and optional password.
  • Discord, Telegram, GitHub, feedback and support routes extend the community surface.

Capability boundary

The room browser displayed three regions and official rooms at zero occupancy, while the public creator description says human multiplayer was not implemented in the indexed build. Treat the lobby as a discoverable service surface whose end-to-end human play is unverified. Never market “live multiplayer” until join, replication, authority, disconnect and reconnect paths pass acceptance tests.

Acquisition hook

Instant-access FPS + Brazilian satire + bizarre character thumbnails produces a strong “send this to a friend” premise.

Return hook

Maps, factions, characters and weapon filters create variety. Without unlocks or reliable human competition, return depends on content novelty and self-imposed challenges.

Support loop

A dedicated support panel explains that contributions fund server, domain and improvements. Feedback optionally captures email/newsletter intent.

13

Growth interpretation

The growth thesis is plausible but currently qualitative. Available evidence supports novelty and production velocity, not retention or scale.

What can spread

Zero install removes the handoff cost after a social post. Faction jokes, unusual characters and loud victory imagery create screenshots that explain themselves better than generic gunplay.

What can retain

Seventeen publicly indexed maps, 53 characters and multiple modes suggest breadth. Yet breadth only retains if opponents, difficulty and rules generate meaningfully different matches.

What is not evidenced

No public play count, cohort retention, concurrent-user history or conversion data was available. The home “online” figure changed during the session, but its definition is unknown and must not be treated as CCU.

Measured public footprint

The indexed repository showed 1,668 commits and 34 forks. These are development/community signals, not player traction metrics.

14

Development story & technology

The public repository describes a deliberately agentic production system: multiple models, explicit documentation, browser harnesses and asset-processing tooling around a vanilla game client.

Confirmed public stack

  • Three.js r160, vendored, for the WebGL game layer
  • Vanilla JavaScript ES modules for runtime code
  • Astro SSR for site and API surface
  • Vercel deployment and managed Postgres
  • Playwright quality gates
  • gltf-transform and meshoptimizer for GLB processing

Agent workflow

Public project material attributes work across Claude, Kimi, Codex/GPT and GLM, with agent labels in commits. The owner coordinates the system and maintains executable constraints, browser harnesses, documentation and task-specific skills.

Engineering pressure

The hardest problems are not polygon count alone: network authority remains unverified, global ranking is feature-flagged off while telemetry continues, and hundreds of assets/scripts amplify integration and provenance risk.

Iteration evidence

The project was renamed from CS BRASIL to CORO SOLTO, and public documentation was corrected to distinguish the Three.js game client from the Astro SSR site. That is healthy evidence of architectural clarification. The observed UI identified itself as a slightly newer alpha build than the indexed Radar snapshot; exact version parity should not be assumed.

16

Reconstruction blueprint

Reconstruct around deterministic match state and capability truth. The visual shell is straightforward; round authority, input ownership and service-state honesty are the load-bearing parts.

Client state machine

Boot→Home→Setup: match→Faction→Character→Opponent→Load→Round live→Round result↺Match result

Global overlays—settings, pause, scoreboard, profile—form a separate stack over allowed base states. Each overlay declares whether it captures pointer, keyboard and simulation time.

Core data contracts

  • Profile { id?, nickname, links[], localStats }
  • MatchConfig { mode, mapId, weaponFilter, teamSize, roundCount, winCondition }
  • Faction { id, name, slogan, color, characters[] }
  • Character { id, role, rarity, stats, model, voiceSet }
  • MatchState { phase, round, clock, scores, players, events }
  • Capability { multiplayer, ranking, telemetry, regions }
P0

Authoritative simulation

Use a fixed-tick match core. Server authority is mandatory for human play; bots may run server-side or in an identical deterministic host. Damage, respawn, score and round end emit ordered events.

P0

Input & overlays

A single input router owns pointer lock. Opening an overlay releases it; closing restores it only after explicit click. Tab scoreboard is hold-to-view and cannot fire weapons beneath it.

P0

Rules as configuration

Help copy, setup summary, HUD and result text all render from the same validated rules object. Fixed rounds and best-of must be distinct modes.

P1

Content manifests

Maps, weapons, factions and characters load from versioned manifests with stable IDs, localization keys, model budgets and fallbacks. Missing art never blocks navigation.

P1

Persistence

Write local stats after an idempotent match-final event. If global ranking is disabled, never enqueue rank UI; telemetry failure must not block results.

P2

Service resilience

Region ping probes run concurrently with timeout. Lobby preserves last good data, labels freshness, exposes retry, and rejects outdated responses after region changes.

17

Acceptance specification

The clone is acceptable only when visible states, rules and failure paths are testable. Screenshot similarity alone is insufficient.

P0

Solo happy path

Given a fresh local profile, when the player sets a nickname, configures a 2v2 fixed five-round Deathmatch, selects faction/character/opponent and starts, then the chosen configuration and identity appear in match state and all five rounds can resolve into one result.

P0

Round authority

Given fixed-round mode, when one team becomes mathematically unbeatable early, then remaining rounds still run. Given best-of mode, the same state ends immediately. Help and HUD must match.

P0

Death/respawn

When health reaches zero, then firing and movement stop, killer/weapon/range/direction recap appears, respawn countdown completes once, and the player returns with configured health and protection state.

P0

Score integrity

When ordered kill events arrive, then kill feed, player kills, team score, streak and round table reconcile. Duplicate event IDs do not increment any counter twice.

P0

Pointer ownership

When settings, pause or held scoreboard opens, then camera input cannot leak through. Closing a modal restores play only after the required pointer-lock gesture.

P1

Settings persistence

When quality, sensitivity, axis, volume, voice, language and crosshair change, then Apply updates live where safe, Save survives reload, and Restore Defaults returns schema defaults.

P1

Pickup & inventory

Given overlapping dropped weapons, when aim changes, then exactly one candidate is named. Pressing E performs one deterministic replacement and updates weapon/ammo HUD.

P1

Lobby truthfulness

Given multiplayer capability is false or unhealthy, then Quick Play and Join explain the limitation and do not simulate success. Empty, loading, stale and failed lists remain visually distinct.

P1

Result transaction

When match-final commits, then rounds, kills, deaths and local stats update exactly once. Replay retains config but creates a new match ID.

P2

Accessibility/responsive

At 1280×720 through 2560×1440 and 200% browser zoom, then menu actions, setup controls and results remain reachable; color is never the only selected/team indicator; reduced-motion removes banner scaling.

18

Experiments

Prioritize tests that convert identity and breadth into confident first-match completion before adding more content.

E1

Practice presets

Hypothesis: a three-choice difficulty card before bot count improves completed matches without diluting setup freedom. Measure setup→load conversion, round completion and replay rate.

E2

Rule sentence

Hypothesis: replacing “5 rounds” with “Play all 5 rounds” or “First to 3” reduces early exits and help opens. Measure rule-help opens and exits after the third round.

E3

Character consequences

Hypothesis: concrete role effects beneath abstract bars increase character exploration. Measure preview depth, selection distribution and post-match character changes.

E4

Shareable result

Hypothesis: a privacy-safe faction result card with map, score and streak creates organic sharing. Measure card generation and verified referral landings.

E5

Honest lobby gate

Hypothesis: labeling rooms as “network preview” until end-to-end readiness preserves trust better than clickable dead ends. Measure failed joins, back-outs and feedback sentiment.

E6

Local-stat re-entry

Hypothesis: after match one, home should show a compact personal best and “beat it” CTA. Measure second-match start within the same and next session.

19

Confidence & unknowns

Confidence is high for the visible solo path and interface geometry, medium for content-scale claims tied to the public repository, and low for uncompleted network, balance and long-term behavior.

ConfidenceSupported conclusionsOpen questions
HighMain shell, settings categories, local stats, help, setup sequence, faction/character screens, HUD layout, Deathmatch respawn, kill feedback, five-round result, lobby information architectureMinor states not opened; exact breakpoints; focus order; audio mix
Medium53-character roster, 17-map repository content, 26 weapon GLBs, stack/process description, local satire as acquisition hookWhich assets are active/balanced; how different characters materially play; how content changes across versions
LowHuman multiplayer readiness, anti-cheat/authority, Capture behavior in practice, ranking pipeline, population, retention, monetization/support conversionJoin/reconnect/host migration; server economics; public CCU; cohort data; exact scoring/damage/spawn formulas

Evidence discipline

Behavioral statements come from a completed first-session route and supplied interface frames. Public scale, stack and development statements come from the indexed creator/repository snapshot. Product recommendations are explicitly analysis, not claims about hidden implementation.

Do not assume

Do not treat lobby presence as a proven multiplayer match, changing “online” text as verified CCU, repository counts as adoption, character bars as confirmed formulas, or a room/ranking UI as proof of backend readiness.
